question: The plans of certain European operators interested in connecting Barcelona to the rest of Europe by night train have been stopped. The French rail regulator ART and rail operator SNCF do not yet seem able to cooperate.1 SNCF and Spanish railways, Renfe, have said that night trains are not as profitable as high-speed trains.

However, a report showed that most of the proposed routes already exist and would be easily moved from plane to train2. Some of the problems associated with the allegedly low demand for night trains are the high fees operators have to pay for track use, the lack of visibility of new offers on major ticketing and booking platforms, or that the situation varies greatly from one Member State to another.3 1.
In the short term, will the Commission intervene to break the impasse over the Barcelona night train line?
In the medium term, will the Commission push for harmonisation of good practices towards consumers, boosting cooperation between Member States in order to enable effective complaint management?

In the long term, will the Commission set out an EU masterplan for trains, including an EU-wide insurance policy to guarantee consumers access to quality and regular trains, options for passengers to continue their journey in the event of a problem, and clear information available at all times?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.8.2024) 1. The planned night train service Amsterdam – Barcelona is included in the Commission’s cross-border pilot services programme1. The Commission is following this pilot closely.

The Commission intends to promote cooperation between actors and facilitate as much as possible the solution of problems, including easier access to infrastructure for rail operators through appropriate pricing and a more user-friendly ticketing and access to the rail system.

Where railway undertakings consider to be treated unfairly by infrastructure managers, they should address in the first instance the Regulatory Body of the Member State concerned, in this case the Autorité de régulation des transports2 and the Comisión Nacional del Mercado y la Competencia3. 2.

The EU has adopted several regulations to safeguard users’ rights in order to improve the quality and effectiveness of passenger services. Regulation (EU) 2021/782 establishes specific rights for rail passengers4, and in particular obliges Member States to designate a body to handle complaints by rail passengers and includes provisions to foster coordination between national enforcement bodies. 3.

The Commission published an Action Plan to boost long-distance and cross-border passenger rail in 20215 and several of the actions are under way. The preparatory work for a possible initiative on multi-modal ticketing includes considerations on journey continuation in case of delays. Furthermore, Regulation (EU) 2021/782, which applies since June 2023, includes a reinforced right to re-routing for passengers.

Passengers should also receive travel information before and during the journey. To this effect, it introduces obligations for sharing real-time dynamic traffic data and travel information among infrastructure/station managers, railway undertakings, ticket vendors and tour operators.
